Petrov and Macdonald’s RSS is target removal and reconstruction, rather than exponentially sampling ordinary next-item windows. For a sequence of length n, draw c=max(1,⌊τn⌋) positions with replacement, with p(k)=α^(n−k)/Σj α^(n−j). Remove selected positions, preserve the remaining order, and train GRU4Rec’s final sequence representation to predict the selected item set. Duplicate draws collapse; a position’s inclusion probability is 1−(1−p(k))^c. Defaults: τ=0.2, α=0.8, sequence length capped at 50. The paper does not specify a random-window endpoint distribution; its sliding-window discussion describes existing sequence-continuation approaches. [Paper, Algorithm 1 and §5.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2207.02643v2)

Mathematical comparison: for m valid next-item targets in window W, define age a(j,W)=(m−1−j)/(m−1), and w(j,W)=m·4^(−a(j,W))/Σr4^(−a(r,W)). This gives newest:oldest weight ratio 4, preserves causal next-item contexts, and retains every valid target. With window-mean loss, its coefficients equal conditional target-sampling probabilities w/m—but only when sampling leaves inputs unchanged. RSS changes inputs and predicts multiple removed items jointly, so this equivalence does not apply. Its fixed α also gives length-dependent decay; the proposed relative-age decay corresponds to α=4^(−1/(m−1)).

Derived expected interaction coefficient under window-mean reduction is A(t)=ΣW:t∈W q(W)·4^(−a(t,W))/Σr∈W4^(−a(r,W)), where q is the window distribution. Thus overlapping windows accumulate contributions: uniformly sampled fixed-length windows give equal total weight to interior interactions, despite within-window recency preference; boundaries differ. Truncation excludes targets entirely outside sampled windows, while short-window normalization changes included coefficients. Mean-one normalization does not correct overlap or exclusion. RSS’s analogous inclusion exposure sums q(W)[1−(1−p(t|W))^c(W)], before loss-specific normalization; neither procedure guarantees globally exponential per-interaction weights.
